title: Holi: the colors of Braj
hook: the morning after the fire: Krishna, Radha, a handful of color, and lila, God at play
carry: lila: god plays, and love plays back

segments.voice: Yesterday, the night before Holi: the bonfire, and Prahlada walking out of the flames. Your line: bhakti. Prahlada held the name, and it held him.

The fire has burned down to ash. Some people carry a little of it home, still warm, and touch it to their foreheads. The next morning, the street belongs to color. Pink, green, yellow, a purple that won't wash out until Thursday. But why color? Nothing in Prahlada's story is pink. For the colors, people tell a different, smaller story, set in a village by a river, about a boy who was worried about his skin. And that story tells you how to play Holi well.
screen: `THE ASH, CARRIED HOME.` → `WHY COLOR?` → `A SECOND, SMALLER STORY.`

segments.voice: The boy is Krishna, growing up among cowherds in Braj, the country around Mathura and Vrindavan. He's dark; the old poems call his skin the color of a rain cloud. The story people tell is that he goes to his foster mother, Yashoda, upset: why is Radha so fair, and I'm so dark? Yashoda laughs: go and put some color on her face, then. So he does, and Radha and her friends put color right back on him. It's a story families and songs tell, not a scene from an old scripture. But it carries one of Hinduism's big ideas: lila, God's play. In Braj, Krishna isn't a distant king. He's the Lord, and he plays: he steals butter, he dances, he throws color. And in Braj devotion, Radha is the greatest of his devotees, so close in love that the color goes both ways. Holi lets everyone join the game. In Barsana, Radha's village in the stories, women playfully chase the men from Krishna's village with long sticks, and the men hide behind shields and laugh. In Vrindavan, some temples throw flower petals instead of powder. Many people read the morning this way: for a few hours, everyone is the same messy color, old and young, boss and worker, and the distance between people drops. So the manners matter. You start with elders: a pinch of gulal, the soft powder, on their feet, and a bow. You say happy Holi first, and you don't color anyone who's said no. God plays, and love plays back.
screen: `A DARK BOY WORRIED ABOUT HIS SKIN.` · `GO AND COLOR HER FACE, THEN.` · `LILA: GOD AT PLAY.` · `ELDERS FIRST. ASK. THEN THROW.` · then, large: `GOD PLAYS, AND LOVE PLAYS BACK.`

segments.voice: Picture a temple courtyard in Braj on Holi morning, petals and pink powder in the air. If you pray, say Radhe Radhe, the greeting heard all over Braj, and put a pinch of color at Krishna's feet first. If you don't, picture someone you've drifted from: say happy Holi first, wait for the smile, a small pinch of pink on their cheek, and let them color you right back.
Holi. The spring festival: the fire the night before, for Prahlada, and the colors in the morning, for Krishna and Radha.
Your line: lila. God plays, and love plays back. Tomorrow, nine nights begin. Day one hundred forty-two, done.

howItsDone: On Holi morning many Hindus greet elders first with a touch of gulal and a bow, then play with colored powder and water with family, friends and neighbors, sharing sweets like gujiya; in Braj, where the colors recall Krishna and Radha, the celebrations run for days.

notes: The Yashoda/Radha 'why is Radha fair and I'm dark' story is presented as a story families and songs tell, not scripture. Confirm framing.
'The old poems call his skin the color of a rain cloud' (megha-shyama); a common epithet. Confirm.
Lathmar Holi: women of Barsana and men of Nandgaon (Krishna's village). Described without naming Nandgaon. Confirm.
Ash carried home from Holika Dahan and touched to the forehead: a regional custom, not universal. Confirm wording.
Palash (tesu) flowers as a traditional color source. Confirm.
